transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

I’ve gotten into this habit of making myself throw up after I eat, and I can’t seem to stop doing it even though I know it’s not right. It's really embarrassing to admit, but I just don't know how to break this cycle on my own.
Before you make yourself throw up, do you feel like you eat an unusually large amount of food in a short period, along with a feeling that you cannot stop eating?

Yes, that's exactly what happens. On busy nights after work, I'll stand at the kitchen counter and plow through half a pizza, a bag of chips, and leftovers in about twenty minutes. Once I start, it's like a switch flips and I lose all control, shoving food in my mouth even when my head is screaming at me to stop until I feel physically sick.
To help me understand better, what is your current height and weight, and have you recently lost a significant amount of weight?

I don't really know my exact height and weight off the top of my head. I haven't actually lost a significant amount of weight, but my main struggle is doing everything I can to keep the weight from "sticking" and preventing myself from gaining any.
How often do these episodes of overeating followed by throwing up happen, and how many months or years has this been going on?

This has been going on for about five months now, pretty much since I took on the lead tech role at the shop. It happens every week—I'll binge on several nights when I get home and force myself to throw up at least a couple of times a week.
How much do your body shape and weight influence how you judge yourself or feel about yourself as a person?

They pretty much dictate how I feel about myself every single day. If my coveralls feel tight or my face looks puffy next to the younger guys at work, I feel like a complete failure. It makes me feel like I don't even deserve my lead tech spot, no matter how good I actually am at fixing cars.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent episodes of binge eating (eating large amounts of food with a loss of control) followed by inappropriate compensatory behavior (self-induced vomiting) to prevent weight gain. These episodes have occurred multiple times a week for approximately five months. Additionally, the patient's self-evaluation is excessively influenced by body shape and weight. He does not report significant weight loss or being underweight, which rules out Anorexia Nervosa. This clinical picture meets the diagnostic criteria for Bulimia Nervosa (ICD-10: F50.2).
